lesson.title: Confirming Receipt: How TCP's Acknowledgment Numbers Prove Data Arrived
lesson.summary: TCP's acknowledgment number is a cumulative confirmation of how much of the byte stream has been received intact, and it is the core mechanism behind TCP's promise of reliable delivery.
lesson.body:
UDP has no way at all for a sender to learn whether its data ever arrived, and that gap is precisely what TCP's acknowledgment number field is built to close. It is the primary tool TCP uses to deliver on its promise of reliable delivery, working hand in hand with the sequence numbers covered in the previous chapter.

The exact meaning of an acknowledgment number is worth stating precisely, because it works as a cumulative acknowledgment rather than a per segment receipt. An acknowledgment number of N means "I have correctly received every byte up through N minus 1, please send byte N next." It does not mean "I received segment number N," and it does not confirm just one specific byte in isolation, it is a running high water mark over the byte stream defined by sequence numbers. Because it is cumulative, a single acknowledgment can confirm a large batch of previously sent data at once, even when several segments arrived in between the last acknowledgment and this one.

A worked example continues directly from the previous chapter's numbers. The client sent 500 bytes covering sequence numbers 1001 through 1500. Once the server has received all 500 of those bytes intact, it sends back a segment with the ACK flag set and acknowledgment number 1501, telling the client "everything through byte 1500 has arrived, I am ready for byte 1501 next." If the client then sends a 200 byte follow up segment, sequence numbers 1501 through 1700, and it arrives cleanly, the server's next acknowledgment number becomes 1701.

It is worth walking through what happens on loss, because it shows why cumulative acknowledgment matters so much in practice. Suppose that 200 byte follow up segment is lost, but a later segment sent after it does arrive. The receiver cannot advance its cumulative acknowledgment past 1501, because it is still missing byte 1501 itself, so it keeps sending acknowledgment number 1501 again and again, even as later, out of order data continues to arrive. A sender seeing the same acknowledgment number repeated multiple times gets a strong signal that specifically the data starting at byte 1501 needs to be retransmitted, rather than having to guess or resend the entire connection's worth of data.

In practice, acknowledgments are rarely sent as bare, standalone segments in an active, full duplex conversation. They are usually piggybacked onto data segments traveling in the opposite direction, which is visible in the termination example from two chapters back, where the server's own FIN carried an acknowledgment of the client's FIN in that same segment. That is why a single TCP segment very often carries a meaningful sequence number and a meaningful acknowledgment number at the same time, one describing data going out, the other confirming data that came in.
